summary: This paper evaluates the feasibility of using quadruped robots, specifically the Unitree Go2, for automated tasks in roof environments. Using a custom-built test rig with standard roof tiles, the authors found that standard ball feet are inadequate for sloped roofs, with slippage increasing quadratically and critical failures occurring regularly at a 25-degree incline. The study concludes that safe roof locomotion will require a combination of terrain-aware control strategies and customized foot designs.

chk_data.paper_excerpt:
Evaluating Quadruped Locomotion in Roof
Environments

In roof environments, quadruped locomotion performance is primarily determined by two factors: friction and stability. To objectively evaluate and compare quadruped locomotion, an accurate measurement methodology is required.
In this work the main focus is placed on friction as the primary performance
indicator, while loss of stability, referred to as critical failure, marks the upper
performance limit when the robot falls. Friction can be estimated by measuring
slippage on a defined incline angle. This necessitates an external measurement
system. For this purpose, the OptiTrack system – a motion capture system based
on infrared light and reflective markers – is employed. The system can be calibrated to achieve a measurement accuracy of below 1.0 mm [13].
The feet of a quadruped robot are the primary, and often only, components
that directly interact with the environment [10]. While other end-effectors in
robotics, such as hands and grippers, have received considerable attention, the
development of non-humanoid feet has received less focus [4, 5]. Currently, most
major manufacturers and research institutes employ a simple round foot geometry [9, 14]. This design is widely adopted due to its simplicity, robustness, and
reliable performance across diverse environments [9]. Further, the ball-shaped design allows for a simplified contact modeling approach, reducing the simulated
contact to a point or line [5]. However, such feet provide a limited contact area,
resulting in high stress concentrations and an increased risk of slippage, particularly on inclined surfaces, as rubber friction is area dependent [9, 14, 15]. Moreover, ball feet lack adaptability to varying terrains, restricting their effectiveness
in complex environments [14]. Due to these drawbacks and the highly difficult
roof environment, the development of customized and environment adapted feet
is worth investigating in future work.

4

(1)

To objectively assess the performance of the Go2 (software version 1.4.4) and
create a baseline for future comparison with custom feet, an adjustable test
rig of a roof environment was developed (see Fig. 1). As surface material the
Frankfurther Pfanne was chosen, which is the most common type of roof tile in
Germany [2]. With the Go2, three core skills were examined: balancing on continuously increasing inclines, get-up/lie-down sequences, and incline walking. To
create statistical significance every experiment is repeated ten times. For balancing, the robot was placed facing uphill on a 0◦ incline, which was gradually
increased until balance was lost, revealing failure modes under static conditions.
Get-up and lie-down performance was assessed on progressively steeper inclines
in three orientations (uphill, downhill, sideways), with success defined as completing both actions in each configuration. Incline walking was evaluated by
repeatedly ascending increasingly higher slopes while measuring slippage using
the OptiTrack system to track reflective markers positioned at the sides of the
ball feet. Slippage of the front and rear feet, SFLF/RLF , was defined as the cumulative incremental marker displacement opposing the walking direction X.
The incremental displacement was calculated as ∆xi (t) = xi (t + 1) − xi (t), and
only backward movements were accumulated. To exclude movements during the
swing phase, only increments with negligible vertical displacement, defined as
|∆zi (t)| < ztol = 1.0mm, where ∆zi (t) = zi (t + 1) − zi (t), were considered. The
resulting slippage calculation is given in Eq. (2).

chk_primary_result.paper_excerpt:
Machine Intelligence and Robotics Lab at Karlsruhe Institute of Technology (KIT),
Germany
dettmar@kit.edu

Abstract. This paper investigates the feasibility of deploying quadruped
walking robots for the automation of work in roof environments. While
quadrupeds have demonstrated versatility across various domains, their
large-scale deployment remains limited, partly due to lack of applicationspecific designs. Roof environments represent a novel and unexplored
use case, combining high safety risks for human workers with repetitive,
strenuous tasks that could benefit from robotic assistance. A dedicated
test rig of a roof’s surface was designed to evaluate the baseline performance of a commercial quadruped, the Unitree Go2, in this new environment. Experiments revealed that standard ball feet are inherently
inadequate for locomotion on sloped roofs: slippage increased quadratically with incline angle, get-up and lie-down sequences were only possible
on small inclines, and critical failures already occurred regularly on moderate inclines of 25◦ . This work provides the first systematic assessment
of quadruped locomotion in roof environments, highlighting both the
potential and the current limitations of this application and establishes
a baseline for future research. Effective solutions will require a combination of task-oriented foot designs, advanced contact mechanics and
environment-specific control strategies, such as reinforcement learning
for roof-adapted gaits.
Keywords: walking robots, quadruped, roof environment, construction,
locomotion, friction, stability, motion capture

Fig. 1. Examples of the Unitree Go2 on the test rig while balancing (left), walking
(middle) and overview of the test rig setup (right).

Baseline Results

Overall, the results indicate that, without significant modifications, the Go2 is
not suited for operation within roof environments. Manufacturer claims of slopeclimbing capabilities of up to 40◦ were not achieved under the test conditions [18].
The coefficient of friction for a rubber ball foot on a roof tile was measured
at 1.144 ± 0.1299 on flat and 1.430 ± 0.1298 on curved sections of the roof. Using
Eq. (1), this leads to respective maximum material specific incline angles ρ of
(48.84 ± 3.22)◦ and (55.03 ± 2.44)◦ .
For standing on an incline, the critical angle was measured at (27.58 ± 0.72)◦
on average. Failures were primarily caused by automatic limb repositioning,
which appears to be triggered by slippage of individual limbs or atypical joint
angles.
Get-up and lie-down experiments revealed additional limitations. Full task
success was achieved only at low inclines: up to 11.0◦ for head-up and head-down
orientations, and up to 7.0◦ for the sideways orientation. In all cases, failures
occurred when the center of mass (COM) exited the support polygon during the
pre-programmed motion.
Incline walking performance was quantified by measuring mean slippage, calculated from positional data of reflective markers on front and rear feet. The
robot was tested on inclines ranging from 0◦ to 25◦ , with frequent falls observed
at 25◦ . Experiment runs that ended in critical failure were excluded from later
statistical analysis. Example trajectories of the experimental setup are provided
in Fig. 2. The tracking data of each run in the roofs surface coordinate system
is depicted in Fig. 3.
The first column of Fig. 3 shows the absolute position of the front left foot
(FLF) and rear left foot (RLF) in the walking direction (X -direction). As the
robot starts on flat ground, the first second of the plots is very similar, independent of the current inclination. The overall trajectory does change with higher
inclines, though. On steeper slopes, slippage – especially of the rear foot – can be
identified in areas where the absolute position decreases. The detected slippage
is not a continuous sliding of the foot but rather an abrupt slip-off, often followed by an instantaneous follow-up step to regain ground contact. Furthermore,
the plots show a greater variation in runtime. As the robot needs to rebalance
more on higher inclinations, full standstill is sometimes reached later. The X -

drafts.paper_quote: Regression analysis revealed a highly significant (p < 0.0035) linear relationship between incline angle and traveled distance, a highly significant (p(F ) < 0.001) quadratic relationship between incline angle and slippage, but no explainable correlation between incline angle and trajectory deviation.

direction plots also show that the roof environment makes the robot slip even on
flat ground, due to the small steps between individual rows of tiles. When the
robot steps on the edge of one of these steps, the foot can easily slip off, either
during initial placement or at the start of the next step when the foot rotates
forward and pushes off. Lastly, increasing the incline angle leads to a decrease in
total traveled distance. This can be directly calculated from the diagram data,
as the X -direction is always set to be in-plane with the roof’s surface, and distance measurements for calculation start only when all four feet are on the roof –
cutting off the part on the palette where movement is not directly in X -direction
for incline angles above 0◦ .
The second column shows the deviation in Y -direction, perpendicular to
the X -direction. These graphs indicate how well the robot maintains its given
trajectory. Generally, the robot does not walk perfectly straight, even on flat
ground. This can be seen in the beginning of the trajectory: starting on flat
ground, both the FLF and RLF drift to the right, probably due to accelerationinduced imbalances. The roof environment further increases trajectory deviation,
as the curved areas of the tiles promote slippage in Y -direction. An increase in
incline angle seems to correlate with greater trajectory deviation. Additionally,
the robot might change its orientation on steeper inclines, as observed by the
RLF drifting to the left side while the FLF drifts to the right side.
The third column depicts the robot’s gait pattern in Z -direction. The horizontal areas of the graphs show phases in which the foot stays on the roof’s
surface. These horizontal areas increase with each first or second step, indicating that the foot is placed on the next row of tiles. Because the ground plane
is always set to align with the lowest row of tiles, an increase in incline angle
leads to an initial decrease in the Z -position, as the Z -axis points partially into
negative X -direction on flat ground. The increase in incline angle also correlates
with a smaller increase in height, as the robot does not walk as far. Furthermore,
the plots show greater variance, as the robot slips more often and deviates from
its standard gait pattern.
